summary: Connect counting to how many there are, for quantities up to 20.
Use ordinal words, first through tenth, to tell position and order.
Count to answer "how many?" for up to 20 objects in a line, array or circle, or 10 scattered.
Given a number from 1 to 20, count out that many objects.
Add and subtract numbers within 10.
Solve adding and taking-away word problems within 10, using objects or drawings.
Copy, continue and make simple patterns with real objects.
Build and break apart 11 to 19 as ten ones and more ones; recording each is not required.
Explore pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters, and begin to recognize pennies and dimes.
Compare and sort flat and solid shapes of any size or turn, describing their parts informally.
Add and subtract within 20 using strategies like counting on, making ten and known facts.
Add and subtract within 10 fluently.
Name pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters, know their values, and write amounts with the cent sign.
Count a mix of dimes and pennies and give the total in cents, up to 100 cents.
Solve one-step adding and subtracting word problems within 100, with the unknown in any position.
Begin working on two-step adding and subtracting word problems within 100.
Add and subtract within 20 fluently using mental strategies such as making ten.
Know all sums of two one-digit numbers from memory.
Tell whether a group of up to 20 objects is odd or even, by pairing or counting by 2s.
Write an even number as the sum of two equal addends.
Add and subtract within 1000 with models, drawings or place-value strategies, and record the strategy.
Understand that adding or subtracting three-digit numbers combines like places, regrouping tens or hundreds when needed.
Count a mixed set of coins worth up to one dollar.
Solve money problems within one dollar using coins and the cent sign; no dollar bills or $ sign.
Sort flat shapes into polygons and non-polygons.
Fluently multiply one-digit numbers and do the related divisions, using strategies.
Know all products of two one-digit numbers from memory.
Solve two-step word problems with whole numbers using all four operations.
Write equations or expressions with a letter for the unknown in two-step problems.
Check two-step answers using mental math and estimation, including rounding.
Find and continue number patterns, including patterns in addition and multiplication tables.
Understand four-digit numbers as thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
Read and write four-digit numbers in numerals, words and expanded form.
Measure and estimate liquid volume and mass in grams, kilograms and liters.
Solve one-step word problems about masses or liquid volumes in the same units, with any operation.
Find the area of shapes made of non-overlapping rectangles by adding; at most one unknown side.
Find a polygon's perimeter from its sides, or one missing side from the perimeter.
Find rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas, or the same area but different perimeters.
Name and sort polygons by sides and vertices (triangles to hexagons), and spot shapes that fit none.
Solve multistep whole-number word problems with all four operations, including interpreting remainders.
Write equations or expressions with a letter for the unknown in multistep problems.
Check multistep answers using mental math and estimation, including rounding.
Read and write multi-digit whole numbers in numerals, words and expanded form.
Compare multi-digit whole numbers by place value using >, = and <.
Know sizes of ft/in and km/m/cm; convert larger units to smaller with known or given factors; make tables.
Solve word problems about distance, time, liquid volume, mass and money with all four operations.
Include measurement problems with fractions or decimals, and converting larger units to smaller ones.
Show measurement quantities on diagrams with a scale, such as number lines.
Name triangles by their angles: right, acute or obtuse.
Identify every quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides as a parallelogram.
Identify every quadrilateral with four right angles as a rectangle.
Use the order of operations to evaluate expressions; no exponents or nested grouping symbols.
Find a rectangular prism's volume by packing unit cubes and link it to multiplying edge lengths.

state_code: # SOURCES (New York State Next Generation Mathematics Learning Standards, 2017; crosswalks updated June 2019)

# - https://www.nysed.gov/sites/default/files/programs/standards-instruction/nys-next-generation-mathematics-p-12-standards.pdf  (official P-12 standards; used to confirm codes and sub-part structure)
# - Row text was read from the NY column of the official 2011-CCLS vs NGLS crosswalks and compared to CCSS 2010 (not to NY's 2011 CCLS, which already had NY additions such as coins in 1.MD.3).
# CCSS K-5 STANDARDS DROPPED: none entirely. Partly dropped or narrowed:
# - 2.G.A.1: drawing shapes with given angles/faces and identifying cubes dropped; polygon naming moved to NY-3.G.1; NY-2.G.1 is polygon vs non-polygon.
# - 3.G.A.1: quadrilateral sub-category work moved to NY-4.G.2b/2c and NY-5.G.3 (inclusive trapezoid).
# - 4.G.A.2: classifying by perpendicular lines / right triangles as a category narrowed to NY-4.G.2a-c.
# - 2.MD.C.8: dollar bills and the $ sign removed in grade 2 (cents only).
# - 5.OA.A.1: brackets/braces and nested grouping removed (order of operations without exponents instead).
# - 5.MD.C.5a: threefold products / associative property clause removed.
# - K.NBT.A.1: recording each composition by drawing or equation removed.
# - 4.MD.A.1: knowing relative sizes is limited to ft/in and km/m/cm; other conversion factors are given.
# - Pre-K (NY-PK...) rows are omitted (no CCSS counterpart; grade column is K-5 only).
# - NY-1.MD.3b/3c (coins in grade 1) are marked "moved" from 2.MD.C.8; NY-3.NBT.4a/4b (four-digit place value) are marked "moved" from 4.NBT.A.2. Both are judgement calls.
# - NY-3.G.1 is mapped to 2.G.A.1 (polygon names) plus 3.G.A.1; kind "moved" is a judgement call.
# - Added vocabulary (o'clock/half past, quarter past/to in NY-1.MD.3a, NY-2.MD.7) and NY "Notes" that restate CCSS footnotes were treated as "same".
# - CCSS baseline: CCSS Math PDF, https://corestandards.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/Math_Standards1.pdf ; ccss codes are expanded with cluster letters from the CCSS K-5 list.
# - kind is judged on content, not code: a state standard that only renames/recodes or drops/moves examples into notes is "same".
# - Lettered sub-parts get their own row (with a stem row when the stem has its own text). A sub-part that mirrors a CCSS sub-part is "same";
#   a sub-part carved out of a CCSS standard that has no such sub-part (e.g. a split of one CCSS sentence into a/b) is "edited" with a summary.
# - Sub-part rows list the parent CCSS code (CCSS sub-part letters are not used in the ccss column).
# - "moved" is used when the main content comes from another CCSS grade; the other grade's code is in ccss.
